legend: You are the host of a large tournament that will feature $$$k$$$ athletes. You have $$$n$$$ familiar athletes, and you want to invite some of them to participate in a tournament. For each athlete, you know their strength and endurance (let's denote the strength of the $$$i$$$-th athlete as $$$p_i$$$ and their endurance as $$$s_i$$$). The $$$j$$$-th athlete will definitely defeat the $$$i$$$-th athlete only if they are strictly stronger and more enduring (i.e., if $$$p_j  \gt  p_i$$$ and $$$s_j  \gt  s_i$$$); otherwise, either of them could win.

The tournament proceeds as follows: as long as there are at least two athletes remaining, a pair is formed from two randomly selected athletes who have not been eliminated, the winner stays in the tournament, and the loser is eliminated. This continues until a tournament winner is determined.

To make the tournament as spectacular and unpredictable as possible, you want to invite a set of exactly $$$k$$$ athletes such that the winner is not predetermined. In other words, for a fixed set of $$$k$$$ athletes and considering all possible outcomes of pairwise wins and losses, there will be at least two outcomes where tournament winners are different.
Before finalizing the tournament lineup, you want to determine how many suitable sets of exactly $$$k$$$ athletes exist.
input: The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \le k \le n \le 5000$$$) — the number of athletes and the size of the tournament.
The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n$$$ ($$$1 \le p_i \le 10^9$$$); where the $$$i$$$-th integer represents the strength of the $$$i$$$-th athlete.
The third line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$s_1, s_2, \dots, s_n$$$ ($$$1 \le s_i \le 10^9$$$); where the $$$i$$$-th integer represents the endurance of the $$$i$$$-th athlete.
output: In a single line, print a number — the amount of suitable sets of exactly $$$k$$$ athletes. Since the answer may be quite large, output it modulo $$$998\,244\,353$$$.
